title: The last hour
hook: bright screens late tend to push sleep later

segments.voice: Yesterday, the practice underneath every practice. Your line was go to bed. Did you keep your bedtime, or did one more episode win? Either way, day one hundred thirty-six.

For almost all of human history, the last hour of the day looked about the same everywhere. The sun went down. There was firelight, maybe a lamp, then the dark. Then, in a blink, we got electric light, then television, then a bright little screen we hold six inches from our faces in bed. Your body's clock is much older than any of that, and it still reads light as a message: it's daytime, stay up. So if yesterday you picked a bedtime, today is about the hour before it, the runway sleep lands on. Today's practice is the last hour.
screen: `FIRELIGHT, THEN THE DARK.` → `A BRIGHT SCREEN IN BED.` → `THE LAST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the mechanism, in plain words. As evening comes and light fades, your brain starts releasing melatonin, a hormone that tells the body night has arrived. Bright light, especially the bluish light screens and many bulbs give off, can hold that signal back. In the early two thousands, scientists found special cells in the eye whose main job isn't seeing shapes at all. They measure light, and report to the body's clock. Then came a study at Harvard, published in 2015. For five nights, people read on a light-emitting e-reader before bed; for five other nights, they read a printed book. After the screen, they took longer to fall asleep, their melatonin came later, and they felt less alert the next morning. That's a lab study with a small group, so it's a clue, not a verdict. And light isn't the only thing: a gripping show or a tense group chat wakes the mind up too, whatever the color of the screen. Night mode helps a little; it doesn't make the scroll restful. So the practice here is gentle and old. Let the last hour look a bit more like the old evenings. Lamps instead of overhead lights. Screens off, or at least far away. Something slow in your hands: a book, a cup, a conversation, a stretch. You're not fighting the day. You're dimming it, the way the sky does, a little at a time.
screen: `MELATONIN RISES IN THE DARK.` · `CELLS THAT MEASURE LIGHT.` · `E-READER VERSUS BOOK, 2015.` · `LAMPS, SLOW THINGS, SCREENS AWAY.` · then, large: `DIM THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan tonight's last hour. Settle, and breathe. Take your bedtime from yesterday and count back one hour. Picture that moment: which lights go off, and which lamp stays on? Where does the phone go, charging in another room, or face down across the room? What slow thing will you hold instead? See it clearly, as if it's already evening. The bell holds the time.
The last hour. The runway before sleep, when dim light and slow things let the body's clock say night. Today's word.
Your line: dim the day. Tonight, an hour before bed, turn the lights low and put the screen out of reach. Say your line as you do it. Day one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Sleep specialists often suggest a wind-down hour before bed with lower light, fewer screens and a calm routine, sometimes called sleep hygiene.

trapdoor: what you thought: screens keep you up because of what you're watching.
what it means: that too, but bright light itself tells the body's clock it's still day.
what a scholar hears: light-sensing retinal cells (described around 2002) signal the clock; Chang and colleagues' 2015 e-reader study found delayed melatonin and sleep.

sources.ref: Chang et al. (2015), Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, PNAS 112(4)
Berson, Dunn & Takao (2002), Science 295; intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells

notes: Chang et al. 2015 (Brigham and Women's / Harvard): confirm five nights each condition, later melatonin, longer sleep latency, lower next-morning alertness, and small sample.
ipRGC discovery dated to around 2002 (Berson et al.; Hattar et al.): confirm the 'early two thousands' framing.
'Night mode helps a little' is a hedge; evidence on night-shift modes is mixed. A reviewer may prefer 'may help a little'.
